story.title: Cargo Jet Attempted to Abort Landing Before Fatal Miami Crash
story.summary: Flight data indicates that an Amazon cargo plane attempted to abort an unsteady landing at Miami International Airport before crashing into a van, resulting in the deaths of five individuals inside the vehicle. The victims were identified as employees of a cleaning service contracted by airlines. Two additional people were reported to be in critical condition following the incident.

event_overview.title: About Fatal Amazon Cargo Plane Crash at Miami International Airport
event_overview.subject: Fatal Amazon Cargo Plane Crash at Miami International Airport
event_overview.summary: On September 6, 2026, a Boeing 767 cargo flight operated by 21 Air for Amazon overran a runway after arriving at Miami International Airport from San Juan, Puerto Rico. The aircraft struck ground vehicles and caught fire; five people were killed, and the crash is the subject of a federal safety investigation whose cause had not been determined as of September 8.

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: The accident occurred at about 2 p.m. local time on September 6, 2026, at Miami International Airport in Miami, Florida.

facts.label: Flight and aircraft
facts.value: FAA identified the flight as 21 Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft that had departed Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

facts.label: Casualties
facts.value: Five people were killed after the runway overrun struck ground vehicles; authorities also reported injuries. Reporting on September 8 said those killed were occupants of a van used by plane cleaners.

facts.label: Investigation
facts.value: The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating. Its process gathers evidence before issuing a final report that determines probable cause, so early facts should not be treated as conclusions about why the crash occurred.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the initial fatal crash and the next-day investigation developments, not the full recovery, airport-operations impacts, victim identifications, or the eventual NTSB findings.

explore_lenses.label: What do the preliminary flight data show?
explore_lenses.title: A late, incomplete abort is under review
explore_lenses.summary: Preliminary information points to an attempted go-around during an unstable landing, followed by an unsuccessful effort to stop. That sequence is not a finding of cause: investigators still need cockpit-recording context and crew interviews.

claims.text: NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said flight data indicated the crew appeared to briefly attempt a go-around, then abandoned it and tried to stop; the data showed thrust reversers were not used.
The NTSB reported the aircraft traveled about 1,300 feet beyond the runway end; the agency's investigation page identifies the event as a runway overrun during landing on Runway 30.

Former FAA official Mike O'Donnell said the touchdown on the nose and right landing gear appeared consistent with an unstable landing and that the crew may have delayed the go-around; this is expert interpretation, not an NTSB conclusion.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: Investigators have not determined why the go-around was discontinued, why thrust reversers were not used, or whether weather, aircraft performance, crew decisions, or other factors caused the overrun.

explore_lenses.label: Why did an overrun become fatal on the ground?
explore_lenses.title: The aircraft crossed multiple protected boundaries
explore_lenses.summary: The deaths occurred after the overrun extended beyond the runway environment into vehicles on airport property and then beyond the perimeter fence. The crash raises questions about the layout and safeguards beyond Runway 30, but no agency has yet found an airport-safety violation.

claims.text: According to the NTSB account reported by Local 10, the aircraft struck navigational aids and equipment, then a seven-person van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an airline contract-cleaning company; it subsequently breached a perimeter fence and struck an SUV on Northwest 67th Avenue.
All five fatalities were occupants of the cleaning-service van. Two injured people remained in critical condition as of September 8, while the pilot and co-pilot had been released from the hospital.

An airport spokesperson told Local 10 that MIA complies with FAA runway-safety regulations. Separately, the FAA says a standard runway safety area typically extends 1,000 feet beyond a runway end, while EMAS can slow or stop an overrun where that full area is impracticable; neither source establishes whether an EMAS was required or feasible at Runway 30.

explore_lenses.label: What happens in the investigation now?
explore_lenses.title: NTSB evidence review will drive next steps
explore_lenses.summary: The NTSB is leading an active investigation, with the FAA also investigating. Near-term work centers on the crew interviews and analysis of recorded flight and cockpit data; a probable-cause finding is not imminent.

claims.text: The NTSB has launched a go-team investigation into 21 Air Flight 7598, a Part 121 Boeing 767-33A cargo flight from San Juan that overran Runway 30 at MIA on September 6, 2026; its case status is listed as ongoing.
The FAA said it will investigate the runway overrun, and the NTSB said investigators were to interview the pilot and co-pilot on September 9 while reviewing flight-data and cockpit-voice recordings.

Forecast: Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said the NTSB's work is intended to identify the cause and develop future safety recommendations; whether recommendations will be issued, and to whom, depends on the evidence investigators develop.

story_report.summary: An Amazon cargo plane arriving from San Juan overran Runway 30 at Miami International Airport after its crew attempted to abort an unsteady landing, federal investigators said. The aircraft crashed beyond the runway, killing five people in a van used by an airline contract-cleaning service. Two other people remained in critical condition. The National Transportation Safety Board has classified the September 6, 2026, event as a runway overrun and has opened an ongoing investigation.

sections.heading: Flight Data Shows Aborted Go-Around
sections.body: NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said flight data indicated the crew of 21 Air Flight 7598 briefly appeared to attempt a go-around before abandoning it and trying to stop the Boeing 767. The data also showed that thrust reversers were not used. The aircraft traveled about 1,300 feet beyond the runway end, according to the NTSB. Former FAA official Mike O'Donnell said the landing appeared unstable and the go-around may have been delayed, an expert assessment rather than an NTSB finding.

sections.heading: Overrun Struck Cleaning-Service Van
sections.body: According to an NTSB account reported by Local 10, the aircraft struck navigational aids and airport equipment before hitting a seven-person van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an airline contract-cleaning company. It then breached a perimeter fence and struck an SUV on Northwest 67th Avenue. All five fatalities were occupants of the cleaning-service van; as of September 8, two injured people were in critical condition, while the pilot and co-pilot had been released from the hospital.

sections.heading: NTSB and FAA Continue Investigations
sections.body: The NTSB has deployed a go-team to investigate the Part 121 cargo flight and lists the case as ongoing. The FAA also said it would investigate the overrun. NTSB investigators were scheduled to interview the pilot and co-pilot on September 9 while examining flight-data and cockpit-voice recordings. Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said the inquiry is intended to determine the cause and develop future safety recommendations, though any recommendations will depend on the evidence.

unresolved.text: Investigators have not determined why the apparent go-around was discontinued, why thrust reversers were not used, or whether weather, aircraft performance, crew decisions or other factors caused the overrun.

The available record does not establish the cleaning-service van's precise route or authorization, the condition and extent of the Runway 30 safety area, or whether physical mitigation could have changed the outcome.
No final NTSB probable cause, safety recommendation, enforcement action or timetable for a final report has been announced.

related_stories.title: Lindsay Clancy Trial Ends in Mistrial Due to Jury Deadlock
related_stories.summary: The trial of Lindsay Clancy resulted in a mistrial as the jury could not reach a unanimous verdict. A holdout juror expressed reasonable doubt but stated he would not acquit Clancy. Other jurors described frustration during deliberations, revealing that some initially leaned towards a guilty verdict. Clancy's attorney plans to file a motion to dismiss the case following the mistrial.
